# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-16 (Extended v129)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Spring Year 4—Louis Philippe's reign, April 1832)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Rue de la Verrerie (Courfeyrac's residence); Faubourg Saint-Antoine; Faubourg Saint-Marceau; wine-shops (Seven Billiards on Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques; Corinthe on Rue Mondétour; Richefeu's at Barrière du Maine; Café Musain); schools; English provincial towns (Dunstead, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Environmental details**: Frost silvered hedges overnight; chalked crooked sun on forge wall; rain threatened; wind carries salt/tar scent; bees hum in lavender; children chase hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; smoke from chimneys lies flat; gulls quarrel over fish heads in harbor/steps; bees hum; bells ring for vespers; light goes early; river up in spring; baker's boy often late; lines at oven grow long.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, charcoal sketches, moisture. Fireplace with red-hot brazier. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo**: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy). Rope-ladder with hooks, verdigris candlestick.

**WINE-SHOPS & MEETING PLACES**: Centers of revolutionary fermentation. **Seven Billiards (Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques)** and **Café Rue Saint-Hyacinthe**: student rallying points. **Corinthe (Rue Mondétour)**: young men assemble at restaurant wine-shop; secret and public meetings. **Richefeu's (Barrière du Maine)**: marble-workers, painters, journeymen sculptors meet 12-1 o'clock; currently cooling off, playing dominoes. **Café Musain**: Société des Amis de l'A B C affiliated to Mutualists of Angers and Cougourde of Aix. Men openly discuss cartridge-making, plot readiness, armed resistance. Bourgeois visitors in good coats shake hands with "important" men, depart within ten minutes.

**FAUBOURG SAINT-ANTOINE CHARACTERISTICS**: Peopled like ant-hill, laborious, courageous, angry as hive of bees. Quivering with expectation, desire for tumult. Lively yet sombre physiognomy. Poignant distress hidden under attic roofs; rare and ardent minds. Dangerous when distress and intelligence meet at extremes. Population full of proud virtue, capable latent heat, always ready to fly to arms. Powder-house of suffering and ideas at very gates of Paris.

## Marius Pontmercy: Development and Current Crisis
**Identity and background**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction regarding Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Recognized Thénardier in Waterloo painting.

**The Ambush Crisis (resolved with escape)**: Jondrette/Thénardier plotted to extort ransom via girl (Cosette) to lure M. Leblanc. Thénardier metamorphosed from ferocious robber into polished negotiator; devised scheme: wife to dress as before, hunt up "the Lark" (Cosette) with letter; girl would follow into carriage; outside barrier, trap with two horses waits. Young lady to be taken by comrade in other vehicle; wife returns to report. **Threat**: "If you have me arrested, my comrade will give a turn of his thumb to the Lark."

**M. Leblanc's extraordinary escape**: Remained impassive despite brutal assault. Concealed coin piece when searched; unscrewed and used as saw to cut cords. Stretched hand to brazier, **brandished above head the red-hot chisel, emitting threatening glow**. All huddled in amazement. **While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.** Took advantage of confusion and darkness. Dashed out window (door guarded, window not).

**Javert's ambush and action**: Javert (tall man, square face, thin firm mouth, thick gray whiskers) positioned outside with men. Grew impatient, took action before Marius's signal. Ruffians terrified, seized abandoned arms (meat-axe, key, bludgeon, shears, pincers, hammers). Thénardier had knife. **Thénardier woman snatched enormous paving-stone, hurled at Javert's head; Javert ducked; stone struck wall behind.** Javert later quitted building, bearing off prisoners in three hackney-coaches.

**Marius's immediate aftermath (April—precise date unclear)**: Witnessed escape. At nine o'clock evening, betook himself to Courfeyrac at Rue de la Verrerie ("for political reasons"; insurrection-favorable quarter). **Seven o'clock following morning**: returned to hovel, paid quarterly rent to Ma'am Bougon, had books, bed, table, commode, two chairs loaded on hand-cart, departed without leaving address. When Javert returned in morning to question Marius, found only Ma'am Bougon, who answered: "Moved away!" **Two reasons for prompt relocation**: (1) horror of house where he beheld social deformity (wicked poor man, perhaps more terrible than wicked rich man) in most repulsive development; (2) did not wish to figure in lawsuit probable to ensue, be brought to testify against Thénardier.

**Identity and girl recognitions**: Handkerchief bore letters U. F., meaning Urbain Fabre. M. Leblanc is Monsieur Fabre—girl's biological father. Cosette became convent scholar; believes Valjean is her father. **The "girl" Marius worshipped is Cosette, held for ransom by Thénardier.**

## Enjolras and Revolutionary Leadership (Spring 1832)
**Enjolras as nexus of fermentation**: Walking toward organizing mission, passed whole situation in review. Gravity of events self-evident. Descried luminous uplifting beneath gloomy skirts of future. **Believed moment at hand**: people again taking possession of right; revolution again majestically taking possession of France, saying to world: "The sequel to-morrow!" **Content**: furnace being heated. Had at that moment powder train of friends scattered all over Paris.

**Composed network**: Collaborators include Combeferre (philosophical, penetrating eloquence), Feuilly (cosmopolitan enthusiasm), Courfeyrac (dash), Bahorel (smile), Jean Prouvaire (melancholy), Joly (science), Bossuet (sarcasms). Together created sort of electric spark taking fire nearly everywhere at once. All hands to work. **Result would answer to effort.**

**Leadership task**: Need someone to go to Richefeu's (Barrière du Maine) to talk with marble-workers, painters, journeymen sculptors—enthusiastic family but cooling off, thinking of something else, becoming extinguished, passing time playing dominoes. **"Those ashes must be fanned into a glow."** Had counted on "abstracted Marius, who is a good fellow on the whole, but he no longer comes to us."

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## Revolutionary Fermentation and Secret Societies (Spring 1832)
**Public agitation and cartridge-making**: Workmen openly proclaim cartridge-making. Remarks: "In less than a fortnight we shall be parallel with the government. With twenty-five thousand men we can face them." "I don't sleep at night, because I make cartridges all night." Police raids: April 5, agents arrested Pardon at five o'clock in morning while preparing cartridges. Weapons transfer documented. Proclamations addressed to National Guard signed by _Burtot, wine-merchant_: **"Our doctrines are trammelled, our proclamations torn, our bill-stickers spied upon and thrown into prison. The future of nations is being worked out in our obscure ranks. Action or reaction, revolution or counter-revolution. On the day when we cease to suit you, break us, but up to that day, help us to march on."**

**Suspicious activities (April 4, 1832)**: Passer-by mounted post at corner Rue Sainte-Marguerite, shouted: "I am a Babouvist!" Workman warned by "very well dressed man" near canal: "Don't be alarmed, I am an agent of the committee. You are suspected."

**Discovered documents**: Mason left package on bench near bridge of Austerlitz: two printed dialogues signed _Lahautière_, song "Workmen, band together," tin box full cartridges. Ditch between Père-Lachaise and Barrière du Trône: bag with bullet-mould, wooden punch for cartridge preparation, wooden bowl with hunting-powder grains, cast-iron pot with melted lead traces.

**The cipher document (April 15, 1832)**: Carpenter picked up torn papers; extremely significant document bore: Q, C, D, E with instruction: "Learn this list by heart." **Letters meant: quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs [scouts]; date u og a' fe = April 15, 1832.** Under each capital: names with characteristic notes and armaments.

**Secret society network**: Associations of Friends of the People sprang Society of the Rights of Man; engendered Society of Action (impatient individuals breaking away). Other associations: Gallic Society; committee of organization of Municipalities; associations for liberty of press, individual liberty, instruction of people against indirect taxes. Society of Equal Workingmen (divided into levellers, communists, reformers). Army of the Bastilles (cohort organized on military footing: precaution with audacity, stamped with genius of Venice).

**Military infiltration and recruitment**: Army mined at same time as population. Counted on: fifty-second regiment, fifth, eighth, thirty-seventh, twentieth light cavalry. In Burgundy and southern towns, planted liberty tree. Schools as moved as faubourgs.

**Revolutionary fermentation characteristics**: Public, one might almost say tranquil. Approaching insurrection preparing storm calmly. Artery beating everywhere. Network of secret societies spreading like membranes. Not a point in Paris nor France exempt.

## Historical Context: The Restoration and Louis Philippe (1815-1832)
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: House of Bourbon returned after Napoleon fell; believed it bestowed rights, could take back charter rights. Did not understand French society's roots not fixed in Bourbons but in nation.

**Fifteen years of intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Great principles—equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press—worked in perfect peace. Bourbons were instrument of civilization.

**Revolution of July (1830)**: Hardly produced shock; did not treat vanquished royalty as enemy. Mysterious respect springs from events sensing collaboration of someone working above man.

**Louis Philippe (current Spring Year 4)**: Handsome in old age, graceful; not always approved by nation, always by masses. Lacked majesty; wore no crown, no white hair. Mixture of noble and bourgeois suited 1830. Incorruptible; went out with umbrella. Policy domestic rather than national; excessive timidity displeasing to people. Deep tenderness toward family. One daughter, Marie d'Orleans, placed race among artists. Press free, tribune free, conscience and speech free. **Human goodness assessment: will remain one of best princes who ever sat on throne.**

**Cloud gathering (Spring Year 4)**: Strange shade gradually drew nearer, extended over men, things, ideas—shade from wraths and systems. Everything hastily stifled, moving, fermenting. Electric tension such that first comer, stranger, brought light. **Ever since 1830, petty partial revolts suppressed but ever bursting forth afresh—sign of vast underlying conflagration.**

## English Provincial Towns: Population and Daily Life (Wilwick, Kelmere, et al.)
**Population movements (documented)**: Peten Haskick moved to Quenford; Lura Haskick followed. Kadrek moved to Wilholt. Zalis Corrley's daughter settled Wilholt. Kadan Corrley took Yewyn Corrford in marriage at Kelmere. Quiet Jotho married eldest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth at Ostcombe; couple lived there. **That spring, coughing sickness took Nelan; buried at Kelford.** Families involved: Stenworth, Prydenridge, Thornmere, Lindmere, Brackick. **Ulrald Corrford apprenticed anew, became smith.**

**Daily mundane activities (April/ongoing)**: Sorting old letters by candlelight; mending torn sleeves by window, saying little; scrubbing steps while humming childhood tunes. Luena Stenenridge and Rozek Stenenridge talked: "The price of salt is a scandal." Rozek counted coins twice, came up penny short. Rozek pressed jade mirror into hands of wife Rozek Stenenridge, took nothing. Rozek walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Luena laughed at story nobody else found funny. Rorald Lindmere mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Weather, harvest, river conditions constant conversation topics.
